articles.title: Adam Smith's Simple Formula Explains Argentina's Rise, Fall, and Comeback
articles.content:
The December 2026 issue of Reason explores Argentine President Javier Milei's accomplishments and what is yet to be done.
In 1988, the great economist Robert Lucas Jr. asked a simple but haunting question: "Is there some action a government of India could take that would lead the Indian economy to grow like Indonesia's or Egypt's? If so, what, exactly? If not, what is it about the 'nature of India' that makes it so? The consequences for human welfare involved in questions like these are simply staggering. Once one starts to think about them, it is hard to think about anything else."
Adam Smith offered the answer in a 1755 lecture: "Little else is requisite to carry a state to the highest degree of opulence from the lowest barbarism, but peace, easy taxes, and a tolerable administration of justice."
The advantages to peace are obvious. A country won't get rich if foreign tanks are rolling through or if warring factions are killing each other. Resources are diverted from production, specialization, and innovation into fighting. One doesn't accumulate capital for tomorrow if it's likely to be destroyed or stolen.
"Easy taxes" requires a bit of translation to modern language. We instinctively reel from taxes as an imposition on private property, and one that often goes to finance private interests with public means. But we might decide that taxes are necessary to provide security, or even to provide public goods. In order to facilitate economic activity and capital accumulation, those taxes must be predictable and reasonable. They must be sufficiently high to pay for government services but sufficiently low that they don't stifle the economy. For example, in France, government spending stands at almost 60 percent of GDP. This means that, for every euro created by French economic activity, 60 cents are controlled by bureaucrats and politicians, not by individuals, households, and entrepreneurs. By contrast, in the U.S., that amount is closer to 40 percent (about 25 percent federal and 15 percent state and local). In France, the top marginal tax rate on income is roughly 50 percent; in the U.S., it's 37 percent. The U.S. capital gains tax rate is 15 percent (for most earners); in France, the capital gains tax is 30 percent on financial assets and 36.2 percent on nonprimary real estate. Such figures help explain why the U.S. GDP per capita ($90,000) is almost double that of France ($49,000). And France is hardly the world's worst economic actor!
"Tolerable administration of justice" is basically the contemporary concept of rule of law: judicial impartiality, low corruption, respect for contracts, and low executive discretion in administering the laws. Again, the link between rule of law and economic growth is clear. If contracting parties can't be sure that there will be impartial and nonviolent resolutions to disputes, they won't contract, or they'll contract only within their limited circle of trust. If property rights aren't secure, parties will find informal workarounds and not participate in the capital growth of the formal economy. If the government can change rules willy-nilly, people will be hesitant to accumulate capital. (The economist Robert Higgs has shown the role political uncertainty played in the Great Depression lasting so long.)
So there is an answer to the Lucas puzzle. Unfortunately, most countries in the world choose not to apply it. We know how to get there, but those in a position to make the changes benefit from the status quo.
For a case study, consider Argentina. For much of its history, the country endured civil wars (no peace), was poor, and suffered a waltz of dictatorships (no tolerable administration of justice).
After independence in 1816, the country struggled to organize itself politically, causing tensions and strife between different factions. In 1853, Argentina adopted a constitution inspired by the U.S. Constitution. Peace, easy taxes, and a tolerable administration of justice fostered growth. Argentina went from a backwater in 1852 to one of the world's richest countries in 1910.
In the second decade of the 20th century, Argentina turned its back on Smith's advice, first with increased redistribution, then with a series of military coups. Easy taxes and a tolerable administration of justice disappeared, and prosperity waned. Argentina went on to become the International Monetary Fund's biggest debtor.
By 2023, Argentina faced mass poverty and steep inflation. But since then, in three short years, President Javier Milei has made immense strides in improving the economy by returning to Smith's wisdom.
The Spanish colonial crown was not very interested in the area that was to become Argentina.
The area lacked gold and silver, and there was no widespread indigenous population to exploit as labor. The soil was fertile, but this was before refrigeration and trains, so the place couldn't capitalize on cattle exports. What could have been salutary neglect instead became an unhappy combination of heavy bureaucracy (no tolerable administration of justice) and conflict between local strongmen, or caudillos (no peace). By the beginning of the 19th century, Argentina was still a poor backwater.
When Spain fell to Napoleon's armies in 1808, its Latin American colonies faced an existential crisis. Should they give their allegiance to the new crown, to the deposed king, or to themselves (by seeking independence)? Argentina opted for independence, but half-heartedly, and without a clear vision for its post-colonial governance structure.
For the next half-century, Argentina swung between chaos and tyranny. Not surprisingly, the country didn't grow. Caudillos fought each other. From their warfare emerged a stronger caudillo, Juan Manuel de Rosas. He gained control of Buenos Aires, from which he dominated the country from 1829 to 1852. That brought relative peace to Argentina, but his rule did not bring a tolerable administration of justice.
The classical liberal Juan Bautista Alberdi recognized Argentina's need for Smith's recipe. He proposed to get there by combining a strong presidency (to temper the caudillos and maintain peace) with checks and balances (to provide a tolerable administration of justice, instead of tyranny). This, he argued, would attract foreign investment and unleash Argentina's entrepreneurial potential.
When Rosas was deposed in 1852, Alberdi looked to the U.S. Constitution as a model for Argentina. The result was a new constitution of 1853, which established a federal system with enumerated powers divided among three branches.
Smith's prescriptions worked. After three centuries of sputtering, Argentina grew rapidly. By the early 20th century, it was the eighth-richest country in the world.
Under the astonishing growth, Argentina suffered from deep pathologies. Power transfers were peaceful but relied on fraudulent elections by a self-perpetuating oligarchy. Regional caudillos were kept in check by the federal government, but at the price of a strong presidency and weak institutional counterweights. After the opposition broke the oligarchy's hold on power in 1916, there followed 14 years of increasing taxation and income redistribution.
The oligarchy was not pleased. With its support, the military ousted President Hipólito Yrigoyen in 1930—the first of numerous military coups the country suffered in the 20th century. The generals left after reestablishing an oligarch in the presidency. In 1943, the military returned, this time as part of a populist swing. Col. Juan Perón participated in the coup and was rewarded with a ministerial portfolio. As minister of labor, he created an Argentine version of Mussolini's fascism, combining populism, clientelism, corporatism, and the redistribution of public funds to buy votes, with a balance brokered by a powerful state. He was elected president in 1946, and he was reelected in 1951.
Argentina's economy suffered terribly from redistribution and interventionism—the taxes weren't so easy anymore, and the government became a targeted spoils program rather than providing a broad and tolerable administration of justice. As early as 1951, Perón mellowed some of his policies to resuscitate a stagnant economy. Argentina's labor unions, unhappy about losing their privileges, rebelled and some members supported an attempted coup. In 1955, Perón resigned to avert open civil war and went into exile, eventually reaching Francisco Franco's Spain. The military stepped in to replace him.
Argentina then suffered from an unpleasant sequence of Peronist civilian regimes and military coups. After a counter-coup in 1956, the military allowed elections to take place in 1958, but the new government was thwarted by the unions after it cut public spending. In 1962, the military canceled the election results, overthrew the government, then allowed elections to take place in 1963. The military returned in 1966, this time implementing bureaucratic authoritarianism. Labor unrest and subsequent violent crackdowns in 1969 heralded the beginning of Argentina's infamous "Dirty War," marked by the suspension of due process and civil rights. In 1971, a military coup ousted the sitting military government. The 1973–76 civilian government was weak and overwhelmed by a rise of domestic terrorism. Economic reform and cuts in public spending were once again thwarted by strikes. In 1976, the military returned to power and escalated repression of unions and dissidents. From 1976 through 1983, an estimated 30,000 Argentines were "disappeared" by the dictatorship.
Since 1983, the country has again enjoyed civilian rule. But the economic mismanagement continued. Argentina suffered further stagnation and hyperinflation in the 1980s. The situation improved in the 1990s, as structural adjustments and privatizations attracted foreign investment. Argentina seemed to be recovering from its woes. Then foreign debt and domestic spending spun out of hand, and the government defaulted. In 2001, Argentina endured a sharp economic crisis; in the face of civil unrest and economic disaster, it suffered a string of five presidents in less than two weeks.
From 2003 to 2024, Argentina saw a renaissance of Peronism. Institutional counterweights were destroyed. The Supreme Court was packed with presidential allies. A nominally independent central bank became a financing instrument for huge redistributive projects. Statistics were cooked so badly that The Economist simply stopped reporting them for several years. Spending, deficits, and debt soared. Inflation rates started pushing toward 250 percent. The portion of the population living in poverty grew from 10 percent to 45 percent. Having abandoned peace, easy taxes, and a tolerable administration of justice, Argentina had fallen from the highest degree of opulence to the lowest barbarism.
That is the chaos that Javier Milei inherited in December 2023, when he was inaugurated as president of Argentina. Milei, who frequently refers to Alberdi's ideas, moved swiftly back toward Smith's model. He has cut public spending and cut the bureaucracy by 50,000 workers. He has shut down half of Argentina's ministries. He has freed exchange rates and loosened legal tender laws. He has removed rent controls and other contractual impediments to housing. And he has moved to enforce property rights against unionists blocking entry or egress from factories or blocking public ways. (The right to strike, due process, and habeas corpus remain.)
The results are already positive. Annual inflation has fallen from 211.4 percent to roughly 30 percent. The poverty rate has fallen from 45 percent to 28 percent. The Argentine economy grew by 4.4 percent in 2025 (with anticipated growth of 3 percent in 2026). Housing prices have declined by 30 percent in real terms and housing supply has increased by 200 percent. And for the first time in almost 20 years, Argentina is running a fiscal surplus.
Milei's job is not finished. Argentina still suffers from high inflation and regulation. The debt accumulated by decades of Peronism must still be paid off. To prevent future Peronists from resorting again to the monetary printing press, he must shut down the Argentine central bank.
But Milei has already made huge strides. With the application of a timeless formula, he has stabilized, in three short years, an Argentina infected by eight decades of Peronism.
The formula is simple. Peace, easy taxes, and a tolerable administration. Viva la libertad, carajo!
The post Adam Smith's Simple Formula Explains Argentina's Rise, Fall, and Comeback appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: "His Majesty"'s "International Common Law Court of Justice" Threat to "Illuminati Police Forces" Was Criminally Punishable
articles.content:
From State v. McFate, decided Tuesday by the South Dakota Supreme Court, in an opinion by Justice Robert Gusinsky:
Troy McFate gave a law enforcement officer a letter stating certain members of law enforcement would be executed unless they stood down within 48 hours. Construing the letter as a threat, officers initiated an investigation and obtained search warrants for McFate's residence, vehicle, and blood.
Drug paraphernalia was found in McFate's residence and methamphetamine was subsequently found in his blood. McFate asserts the letter was not a true threat and his speech was protected by the First Amendment. A jury convicted McFate of ingestion of a controlled substance, threatening a law enforcement officer, and possession of drug paraphernalia. McFate appeals. We affirm….
At approximately 10:00 p.m. on March 29, 2024, Police Officer Lexy Deneke was completing a traffic stop in Hot Springs, South Dakota. As Officer Deneke finalized the stop from inside her patrol car, she noticed an unknown man standing near her vehicle with a piece of paper in his hand. The man, later identified as Troy McFate, was asked by Officer Deneke to leave the area, but he refused to do so. McFate approached her vehicle and handed her the paper through the car window saying, "You'll see it Monday." McFate left the area, and Officer Deneke finalized the traffic stop before reading the note.
The note contained the following printed message:
DEAR ALL POLICE WORLDWIDE
LET ME MAKE THIS CLEAR WITH EVERYONE WITHIN THE FAKE CORPORATION I YOU HAVE GIVEN YOU 48 HOURS AS FROM TODAY DATE 13TH MARCH 2024 YOU MUST STAND DOWN FROM YOUR CURRENT POSITION WITHIN THE ILLUMINATI POLICE FORCES YOU MUST GIVE UP YOUR WARRANT CARD BECAUSE YOU HAVE COMMITTED CRIMES AGAINST HUMANITY AND YOU HAVE BREACHED YOUR OATH TO THE PEOPLE I WILL MAKE THIS CLEAR WITH YOU THAT IF YOU DON'T STAND DOWN FROM YOUR CURRENT POSITION YOU WILL BE ARRESTED BY UNITED STATES MILITARY AND EXECUTED ON MY ORDER WITHOUT ANY TRIAL DO YOU UNDERSTAND.
YOURS SINCERELY
John Kahlooni
HIS MAJESTY KING JOHN F KAHLOONI JR.
Additionally, in the letter's upper right corner, the original date of "13th March 2024" was crossed out in pen and "4/1/24" was handwritten below it. Accompanying the signature was a printed fingerprint and seal of the "International Common Law Court of Justice." …
The court rejected various challenges by McFate, and in particular had this to say about the threats prosecution:
In this case, the evidence presented at trial was sufficient to sustain a conviction for a violation of SDCL 22-11-15.6. While McFate's defense centered on his testimony that he was attempting to warn Officer Deneke of the impending danger described in the letter, his testimony was inconsistent on this point. During cross-examination, McFate testified that he recognized the threatening nature of the letter and that, but for his "decoding" and modifying of the letter's date, the threat would have passed and there would have been no need to warn anyone. The jury could conclude that McFate had the specific intent to threaten law enforcement given his statement to Officer Deneke when handing her the letter, "You'll see it Monday," a date that would correspond with the 48 hours referenced in the letter in which she would be executed if she did not "stand down from [her] current position."
Ultimately, it was the jury's responsibility to determine the credibility of the witnesses and it is apparent, by the verdict, that the jury did not believe McFate's claim that he was merely delivering a warning. Under the circumstances here, we conclude that there was sufficient evidence to uphold the jury's determination that McFate knowingly and intentionally communicated a threat to take the life of or to inflict serious bodily harm upon a law enforcement officer….
McFate [also] argues that the statute requires the threat to be directed to a specific law enforcement officer. To this point, McFate notes the letter was not addressed to any officer by name, but instead to "the institution of law enforcement." …
SDCL 22-11-15.6 prohibits threats communicated "upon a law enforcement officer." … McFate handed the letter to Officer Deneke and spoke to her when doing so. While the letter was addressed to "ALL POLICE WORLDWIDE" and not directly to Officer Deneke, the statute's plain language does not contain a requirement that the communication be addressed or directed to a specific law enforcement officer…
Assistant AG Jennifer M. Jorgenson represents the government.
The post "His Majesty"'s "International Common Law Court of Justice" Threat to "Illuminati Police Forces" Was Criminally Punishable appeared first on Reason Magazine.

SDCL 22-11-15.6 prohibits threats communicated "upon a law enforcement officer." … McFate handed the letter to Officer Deneke and spoke to her when doing so. While the letter was addressed to "ALL POLICE WORLDWIDE" and not directly to Officer Deneke, the statute's plain language does not contain a requirement that the communication be addressed or directed to a specific law enforcement officer…

Assistant AG Jennifer M. Jorgenson represents the government.

articles.title: Defamation Case by Ex-Husband Against Ex-Wife, Based on Her Allegations to Police, Can Go Forward
articles.content:
Knowingly false accusations about a person made to the police can, in most states, lead to defamation liability. Merely negligently false accusations are usually protected by so-called "qualified privilege": The theory is that people who are unsure about something, or may have misheard or misunderstood matters, should still be encouraged to report matters to the police so that the police—who have better skills and resources to investigate matters—can figure things out. But deliberate lies, which can deceive the police and thus damage their target, are generally unprotected (again, in most states).
Here's an illustration of how this can play out; the opinion, Howard v. Knepp, decided by Colorado Court of Appeals Judge Jerry Jones, joined by Judges Matthew Grove and Timothy Schutz, was just designated as precedential on Wednesday, though it had been issued as a nonprecedential decision in August:
[Ex-husband] Howard and [ex-wife] Knepp were married in January 2014. Seven years later, in January 2021, they jointly filed for dissolution of their marriage. By Knepp's account, "[t]he dissolution proceeding was drawn out and highly contentious."
On March 29, 2022, while the dissolution case remained ongoing, Knepp telephoned the Arvada Police Department to report that Howard had engaged in various acts of fraud. As now most relevant, she told an officer that Howard had opened credit card accounts in her name with Citibank, Vectra Bank, American Express, Capital One, and U.S. Bank without her knowledge or permission. She claimed that she had only learned of those credit cards in December 2020, when she obtained a credit report showing the accounts. Following an investigation and consultation with the First Judicial District Attorney's Office, the Arvada police "determined that there was not enough evidence to continue a criminal investigation into this specific allegation."
In June 2023, Howard filed a complaint against Knepp asserting a claim of defamation and defamation per se. Therein, he alleged that Knepp had made the following false and defamatory statements in her report to the police:
- Howard "had fraudulently opened numerous credit cards in [Knepp's] name."
- "[T]he first [Knepp] knew of these cards was in December of 2020."
- "[Howard] was under criminal investigation for financial fraud of over $1 million in Denver County."
- "[Knepp's] signature had been forged by [Howard]."
With respect to the credit cards, Howard also alleged in the complaint that (1) Knepp knew about them all along because she had opened the accounts herself; (2) various communications showed that Knepp knew about the cards "well before December 2020"; and (3) Knepp knew that Howard hadn't forged her signatures because "she was the one who signed the relevant contracts."
The court allowed Howard's case to go forward:
Knepp argued … that Howard couldn't establish a likelihood of prevailing as to [the relevant elements of defamation] because (1) the credit card allegations were materially true (and therefore not defamatory) and (2) there is no evidence of malice….
With respect to those issues, Howard's affidavit made the following allegations:
- Knepp knew the falsity of the allegations that he had taken out credit cards in her name without her knowledge and that she had only learned of those credit cards in December 2020.
- Knepp "knew that [Howard] had not forged her signature on credit card applications[ ] because she knew that she was the one who signed the relevant contracts."
- He and Knepp didn't keep "separate finances" as alleged in Knepp's motion.
- Knepp signed the Vectra Bank credit card application, contrary to the allegation in her motion.
- Knepp's primary purpose in making the police report was to gain an advantage in the dissolution of marriage case, contrary to the allegation in her motion.
- Knepp didn't believe that the information she gave to the police was "completely true," contrary to the allegation in her motion.
- Knepp was told by credit card representatives that, to be relieved of the debts, she would need to file a police report. (Knepp expressly alleged this in her motion and supplementary affidavit.)
- Knepp and Howard regularly discussed credit reports, and Knepp printed them for reference during their discussions.
- Knepp and Howard both went to U.S. Bank and Vectra Bank to execute documents and verify identifications so that the credit cards would be issued.
- Knepp used the allegations of the police report "to make misrepresentations to the [c]ourt in [the] divorce proceedings" and to other entities.
- Knepp was the primary contact on all the credit card accounts.
In addition, Howard submitted a number of documents, including (1) various emails from Knepp to Howard acknowledging the existence of and approving the accounts as far back as January 2014, and, in at least one case, referring to the card as "my card"; (2) text messages from Knepp to Howard acknowledging and requesting action on the accounts; (3) emails and pictures in text messages sent by Knepp to Howard showing that the account statements were addressed to Knepp; and (4) voicemail transcriptions of messages left by Knepp about messages she had received from American Express and U.S. Bank representatives, which themselves were transcribed. {As well, the police reports and follow-up internal police documentation show that the police had a very difficult time obtaining additional information from Knepp.} …
To be sure, Knepp (via her own affidavit) denied much of what Howard alleged. But her denials and limited supporting documentation don't "defeat[ ] [Howard's] claim as a matter of law." At most, Knepp casts doubt on the veracity of Howard's evidence. At this stage of the case, that isn't enough to warrant dismissal of Howard's claim….
Dan Ernst (Ernst Legal Group, LLC) represents Howard.
The post Defamation Case by Ex-Husband Against Ex-Wife, Based on Her Allegations to Police, Can Go Forward appeared first on Reason Magazine.
